newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN chief sees Iraq oil-for-food deal renewed.
newsitem.headline: UN chief sees Iraq oil-for-food deal renewed.

text.p: U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan said on Thursday that he expected the Security Council to renew Iraq's oil-for-food deal for another six months in June.
Annan also said he expected Baghdad to cooperate fully with U.N. inspectors overseeing Iraq's scrapping of its weapons of mass destruction.
"My expectation is now that we are beginning the scheme, it will continue," Annan told a news conference in Geneva.
"My sense is it will be extended for another six months barring unforeseen developments," he added.

The United Nations gave Iraq clearance in December for limited exports under an "oil-for-food" deal to buy relief aid for Iraqis suffering under economic sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Under the renewable six-month deal, Iraq can sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months.
Annan said he expected there still to be need for food and medicine for Iraq's population of 20 million after the current limited deal expires.
"The need that necessitated the passage of the resolution and the assistance that we are trying to give to the people of Iraq will still be necessary," Annan said.
The U.N. chief also said that it was clear what was expected of Iraq under resolution 687.
Rolf Ekeus, chairman of the Special Commission for the Disarmament of Iraq (UNSCOM), had pressed the point with Iraqi officials, according to Annan.
"The expectation is that they will cooperate fully with the inspectors and work with them in destroying the weapons which are still in the country," Annan said.

"If they cooperate and provide all the evidence and allow them to destroy the weapons or take some of them -- take the necessary material out for analysis, that sort of thing -- I think the (Security) Council will react appropriately," he said.

But Ekeus, speaking to a Washington think-tank on Wednesday, said that weakly worded statements by the Security Council had encouraged Iraq to obstruct U.N. efforts to scrap its weapons of mass destruction.
Iraq had become even less cooperative following a December 30 reprimand from the Security Council, according to Ekeus.
The Council censured Baghdad for refusing to allow more than 100 missile engines to be taken abroad for examination by experts.

UNSCOM was set up after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War but despite six years of inspections and destruction programmes, says it believes Iraq is still concealing ballistic missiles and chemical and biological warfare capabilities.
Annan's remarks on the oil-for-food deal come after some of the toughest remarks against the Baghdad government since U.S. President Clinton took office four years ago.
State Department officials on Wednesday branded Iraqi President Saddam Hussein a "demon" and said there were signs of a power struggle in the country.
